name: Verona Arena
label: Verona Arena
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Bra' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Bra' (way/23964274): middle (383 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/311873: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Verona Arena' (181 m across).
notes: Roman amphitheatre from the 1st century, still used for opera.

text.description:
Verona Arena is a Roman amphitheatre in the historic centre of Verona, and one of the best-preserved ancient amphitheatres anywhere. Restoration work from the 16th century onwards helped it survive in such good shape. Experts still debate exactly when it was built, with suggestions ranging from the 1st to the 3rd century. Scholars' proposals centre on the 1st century, from the late Augustan period to the mid-1st century, which would make it older than the Colosseum in Rome. In summer it hosts an opera festival that has run since 1913, interrupted only by wars, and the rest of the year it works as a concert venue.

It photographs well because the pink-tinted arches fill the frame, with the cafés and arcades of the square around its base giving a sense of scale. For more room for a wide shot, the classic view is from the far side of Piazza Bra. The square is free to stand in, and it is quietest early in the morning. The light is also pleasant in the last twenty minutes before sunset.

For a different view, try the Ponte Scaligero, where the Arena appears in the background across the river Adige. Via Mazzini also offers a view through an archway at the end of the street. Check the framing on the spot, as that last one is less well known.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Verona, on the edge of Piazza Bra, where the Arena fills one side of the square.
text.directions_text: Start from the historic centre of Verona and head for Piazza Bra. From there the Arena is 62 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The far side of Piazza Bra is the classic wider viewpoint if you want more room. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the arches without distortion. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or café tables crowd the foreground and you want more of the curve of the wall. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Bra (far side of the square, facing the Arena). The Arena's pink-tinted arches filling the frame, with the square's cafés and arcades around its base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, so the arches do not lean. Put the base of the wall on the lower line to include some of the square, or keep it tight to the arches for a calmer picture. For a different angle, try the Ponte Scaligero for the Arena across the river, or Via Mazzini for a shot through an archway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arches to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The last twenty minutes before sunset, or early morning when the square is quieter.

text.access_note: The square is open and free to stand in, but going inside the Arena is ticketed and photo rules can change during performances, so check the official site before you go.

name: Juliet's House
label: Juliet's House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'La Casa di Giulietta' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'La Casa di Giulietta' (node/10032080957): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM N7120188585 (Juliet's House): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The famous balcony and courtyard of Romeo and Juliet.

text.description:
Juliet's House is the small courtyard that visitors come to see for its famous balcony. Most people shoot from the courtyard floor, where the crowds gather. From there you can frame the balcony above the courtyard, with the bronze statue of Juliet and the ivy-covered walls in the foreground. It is a tight space, so expect other visitors in your shot. A phone's ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps you fit the balcony, walls and statue into one frame.

There is also a quieter option. Next to the house entrance is an embroidery shop, and a second-floor window there is said to give a raised view down into the courtyard, with the balcony visible from above. You may have the view almost to yourself in the evening when the house is closed. You would be expected to buy a personalised embroidery item to go upstairs. Confirm the shop still offers it.

Access to the courtyard can vary. It may be free, or controlled at busy times, and the courtyard and house may be ticketed through a single entrance at Teatro Nuovo in Piazzetta Navona, with the Via Cappello door reportedly permanently closed. Check the current rules before you go, and allow a little extra time to line up your photo.
text.geographic_location: Juliet's House is in Verona and has a door on Via Cappello, which may be permanently closed.
text.directions_text: Head for Juliet's House in Verona. Plan to reach it on foot. Because the Via Cappello door may be closed, check the official site for the current entrance, which may be at Teatro Nuovo in Piazzetta Navona. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the crowded courtyard to fit the balcony, statue and walls into one frame. From the shop window, use the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, or a telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the balcony from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at La Casa di Giulietta (second-floor window of the embroidery shop next to the house entrance). A elevated, less crowded view down into the courtyard, with the famous balcony visible from above. From there you have two separate options. One is the courtyard floor, with the balcony framed above the bronze statue of Juliet and the ivy-covered walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the balcony on one of the upper intersections. Keep the courtyard below as context. If you are in the courtyard instead, include the statue and ivy at the bottom of the frame so the balcony sits above them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the balcony to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky or bright walls look washed out. If you shoot through a window, hold the phone close to the glass to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the house is closed. The view from the shop window may be quiet then.

text.access_note: Access to the courtyard can vary, so check the official site before you go; the shop window also depends on the shop still offering it.

name: Castelvecchio Museum
label: Castelvecchio
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3210974287: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museo di Castelvecchio'.

text.description:
Castelvecchio Museum is Verona's civic museum, housed inside the medieval castle that gives it its name. The castle itself combines its medieval structure with the 20th-century restoration by the architect Carlo Scarpa. Between 1959 and 1973 Scarpa restored the building. He kept the history of the castle visible and added his own careful details, such as doorways, staircases and fittings. Balancing old and new like this was unusual at the time, though it is now a common approach to renovation. Inside, the collection includes sculpture, paintings, ancient weapons, ceramics and gold work. The collection also includes an equestrian statue of Cangrande I della Scala, which came from the Scaliger Tombs.

Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on gridlines so the castle walls stay straight. If you want to fit in more of the building, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Then try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the masonry and the shapes of the walls. Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky looks washed out. Check current visiting arrangements before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Verona, northern Italy, inside the medieval castle that gives it its name, Castelvecchio.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to find your way. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit the building in, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the castle walls with the vertical lines, keeping the phone level so they don't lean. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then move in with the telephoto for a tighter picture of the stonework and architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits old stonework best. Midday sun can make the shadows harsh.

text.access_note: Check current visiting arrangements before you go.

name: Piazza delle Erbe
label: Piazza delle Erbe
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Torre dei Lamberti' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Torre dei Lamberti' (way/138829597): middle (17 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24400748: 'Madonna Verona', the best-known feature inside 'Herbs Square' (173 m across).
notes: Market square on the site of the Roman forum.

text.description:
Piazza delle Erbe is the old market square of Verona, and it sits on the site of the town's Roman forum. It photographs well because it is lined with frescoed houses and has a bit of everything in one view. In the square is the fountain topped by the Madonna Verona statue. The fountain was built in 1368, but the statue is a Roman sculpture from 380 AD. Along the northern side stand the old town hall, the Casa dei Giudici, the frescoed Mazzanti Houses and the Torre dei Lamberti, which rises above the rooftops. On the western side there is a white marble column with St Mark's Lion, the symbol of the Venetian Republic.

The best-known view over the whole square is from the top of the Torre dei Lamberti. Looking down, you see the market stalls, the fountain, the surrounding rooftops and the River Adige beyond. It is the paid option, so check the official site for tickets and opening times before you go. If you stay at street level, you can still photograph the square for personal use. Shoot along its length with the tower rising above the frescoed facades, or put the fountain in the foreground with the painted buildings and the tower behind. At busy times, vendors, café seating and market stalls can block the view, so be considerate and wait for a gap.
text.geographic_location: Piazza delle Erbe is in the old centre of Verona, on the site of the Roman forum. The Torre dei Lamberti and the old town hall stand on its northern side.
text.directions_text: Piazza delle Erbe is in the old centre of Verona. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so reach the square on foot through the old centre. The Torre dei Lamberti is on the northern side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole square, the stalls and the rooftops into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the fountain and facades. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Madonna Verona statue, the frescoes or the Adige in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Torre dei Lamberti (from the top of the tower, looking down onto the square). An aerial view of the whole square, its market stalls and fountain, with the surrounding rooftops and the Adige beyond. From here, look along the length of the square, with the tower above the frescoed facades. Or put the fountain in the foreground with the painted buildings and the tower behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the tower, turn on gridlines and place the fountain or the line of market stalls on one of the lines. Keep a strip of rooftops and the river in the upper part of the frame. At street level, the ultra-wide (0.5x) works well along the square. For the fountain shot, get low and close, then let the frescoed houses and the tower fill the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the square to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the painted facades and sky keep their detail. Try a short Live Photo of the market for a bit of movement. After sunset, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide recommends sunrise or just after sunset for the view from the tower.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the Torre dei Lamberti is ticketed, so check the official site for current prices and hours before you go.

name: Ponte Pietra
label: Ponte Pietra
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte Pietra' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte Pietra' (way/1525501040): middle (74 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23164367: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Ponte Pietra' (22 m long).
notes: Roman arch bridge over the Adige.

text.description:
Ponte Pietra, the "Stone Bridge", is a Roman arch bridge across the Adige and the oldest bridge in Verona. It was completed in 100 BC, and the Via Postumia from Genoa to Aquileia once ran over it. It also gave the city access to the Roman theatre on the opposite bank. The arch nearest the right bank was rebuilt in 1298 under Alberto I della Scala. Four arches were blown up by retreating German troops in World War II and rebuilt in 1957 using the original materials.

The arches fill the foreground, the river runs away in both directions, and the old-town rooftops sit behind them. The hill by the Teatro Romano rises above the roofs and closes the picture.

For a phone, this is an easy spot. Stand look south-west towards the bridge, and let the arches and the river lead the eye. Be considerate of other people nearby, and take your time. Sunset or golden hour suits it best, and early morning is a quieter option. If you have energy left, Piazzale Castel S. Pietro above the river shows the whole city with the bridge in the middle distance, and the riverbank at Lungadige Re Teodorico shows the arches against the warm-coloured buildings.
text.geographic_location: Ponte Pietra crosses the Adige in Verona and links the city on the right bank with the Roman theatre on the east bank.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the arches, river and rooftops all fit naturally. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arch in the foreground. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the hill and rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte Pietra (mid-span, facing the old town and Teatro Romano hill). The bridge's arches in the foreground with the historic-centre rooftops and the hill behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the line of the bridge along the lower third. Let the river lead the eye towards the rooftops and the hill. If you have time, Piazzale Castel S. Pietro gives a wide view of the whole city from above, with the bridge in the middle distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the river to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At sunset, check the shot is level before you take it. If the light is low, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid support.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or golden hour. Early morning is a quieter option.

text.access_note: Ponte Pietra can be visited without paying, but check the official site before you go. If you also visit Castel San Pietro, the path up is free, but the castle itself is a hotel.

name: Piazza dei Signori
label: Piazza dei Signori
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza dei Signori' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza dei Signori' (way/24403675): middle (99 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W620163456 (Piazza dei Signori): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Elegant medieval square with the statue of Dante.

text.description:
Piazza dei Signori is a square in the middle of Verona, lined with arcaded palace facades, with a statue of Dante standing in the centre. It photographs well because the statue gives you an obvious subject for the foreground, while the arcades and facades around it make a tidy, repeating backdrop. Photos here usually work best as wide shots that show the statue with the buildings behind it.

The cleanest view is from beside the Dante statue, looking down the arcade. From there the statue sits close to you and the line of arches leads the eye away into the square. If you want a second angle, the Arco della Costa frames the square through its archway, and the whale rib hanging from the arch makes an unusual foreground detail. You can also try a tighter, more intimate view of the arcaded side of the square, with the Arco della Costa area behind you.

The square can be busy. Guides say it fills up with the Christmas market in December and with opera-season foot traffic in summer, so you may need a little patience for a clear shot. Late afternoon, when low light falls across the square, is the time guides recommend. Keep your phone steady against your chest, wait for a gap in the crowd, and take a few frames so you can choose the best one later.
text.geographic_location: Piazza dei Signori is a square in the centre of Verona, surrounded by arcaded palace facades. The Arco della Costa, with its whale rib, is next to it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Verona and walk to Piazza dei Signori. Once in the square, find the Dante statue in the middle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Dante statue and the arcaded facades into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza dei Signori (beside the Dante statue in the centre, looking down the arcade). The Dante statue in the foreground with the arcaded palace facades around the square behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the Dante statue to one side and let the arcade lines lead into the picture. Turn on the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For another view, try the Arco della Costa, framing the square through the archway with the whale rib hanging above as a foreground detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facades don't wash out. Portrait mode can help if you want a closer shot of the statue with a softer background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when low light falls across the square.

text.access_note: This is an open square, but events and markets can change how it looks, so expect the square to look different during events and markets.

name: Torre dei Lamberti
label: Torre dei Lamberti
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138829597: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre dei Lamberti' (17 m across).
notes: 84 m medieval tower with the best view over the old town.

text.description: The Torre dei Lamberti is the tall brick-and-stone bell tower that rises above Verona's old centre. It is 84 m high, and building began in 1172. That makes it a good subject for a phone photo, because you can see its long history in the stonework. Lightning struck the top in May 1403, and repairs only started in 1448 and took 16 years. The tower was extended during that work, and the newer sections are made of different materials, including marble. Look for the change in colour and texture. The large clock face was added in 1779. The tower also holds two bells, the Marangona and the larger Rengo. Rengo was once rung to call people to arms or to summon the city councils. The tower is so tall that the main challenge is fitting it in. From close up, it is best to tilt the phone upwards and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), keeping the phone as upright as you can so the sides do not lean too much. If you can step back, the default lens (1x) gives a calmer, more natural view. You can then use the telephoto (2x or more) for a close-up of the clock and the change of materials. Switch on the gridlines to keep the tower straight in the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Verona.
text.directions_text: Head for the historic centre of Verona; the tower is tall enough to spot above the rooftops as you get close. Once you are there, the phone icon on the map is right at the foot of the tower. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the foot of the tower to fit the height in. Use the default lens (1x) when you have stepped back. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock and the change of materials.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph it looking straight up from here. For a fuller view, walk a few steps away from the base and look back up at the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a vertical edge of the tower up with a grid line. Tilt the phone up gently rather than sharply, so the sides lean less. Then take a second shot, zoomed in, of the clock and the point where the stonework changes to marble. Include a little of the buildings beside it to show how tall the tower is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower or the clock to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the stone keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually shows the texture of the brick and stone best. Avoid shooting straight into the sun.

text.access_note: The tower is a visitor attraction, so any climb or entry may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza Bra
label: Piazza Bra
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Bra' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Bra' (way/23964274): middle (383 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23964274: 'Statua Equestre Vittorio Emanuele II', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza Bra' (384 m across).
notes: The largest square in Verona, next to the Arena.

text.description: Piazza Bra is the largest public square in Verona, and it is the natural place to start a photo walk. The Roman Arena fills one side. The Arena, built in the 1st century AD, defined the northern edge of what later became the square. The name comes from 'braida', an old word meaning broad or wide, and that is exactly what you notice when you step out into it. The square has been a favourite for strolling since the Liston, the paved promenade along its edge, was begun in 1770. It still works that way today. Goethe, in his Italian Journey, described crowds walking here. For photographs, the width is what helps you. The open space lets you step back far enough to fit the whole Arena in one frame, with the gardens and the old buildings around it adding a sense of scale. The map's stand-here point is on the far side of the square, looking back across it. Keep the horizon level and let the Arena fill most of the frame. If you have time, walk over to the Portoni della Bra, the double-arched gate. The arches date from the late 14th and mid-15th centuries, and the clock between them was added in 1871. They make a good frame for a second shot.
text.geographic_location: Piazza Bra is in the historic centre of Verona, with the Roman Arena on one side and Palazzo Barbieri, now the city's municipal headquarters, on the eastern edge. The Portoni della Bra gate links it to Corso Porta Nuova.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. From anywhere in Verona's historic centre, head for Piazza Bra, the city's largest square, which is easy to recognise by the Arena. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole Arena across the open square. Then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the arches of the Arena.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Bra (far (east) side of the square, shooting back toward the Arena). The Arena filling the frame across the open square, with the warm stone lit by late sun and the sky behind you going deep blue. From here you look back across the open space towards the Arena. The equestrian statue the map marks lies to the west, in the square itself, so you can include it or leave it out as you turn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the lower line, so the Arena and the sky share the frame. Use the width of the square as foreground, with the gardens and paths leading the eye to the Arena. If the open space looks empty, include a few people walking to give a sense of scale. For a second view, try the Portoni della Bra, using its arch as a frame with the Arena in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the Arena to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the warm stone keeps its colour and the sky stays deep blue. At blue hour, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid support.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The last twenty minutes before sunset, when the stone is warm, or blue hour just afterwards.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but opera and concert nights can bring large crowds and restrict photography, so check the official site before you go.

name: Castelvecchio Bridge
label: Scaliger Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lungadige Cangrande' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lungadige Cangrande nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/116634447: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte Scaligero' (126 m across).

text.description: Castelvecchio Bridge, also called the Scaliger Bridge (Ponte Scaligero), is a fortified brick-and-marble bridge over the Adige, joined to the red-brick Castelvecchio fortress. It photographs well because the whole thing reads as one picture: crenellated walls, three arches of different sizes and the castle rising behind. Its main arch spans 48.70 m, which was the largest bridge arch in the world when the bridge was built, most likely in 1354–1356 for Cangrande II della Scala. The upper part is red brick and the lower part white marble, so the colours stand out against the water. The bridge is about 120 m long. It was destroyed by retreating German troops on 24 April 1945 and rebuilt between 1949 and 1951 by the architect Libero Cecchini. For the classic shot, stand on Lungadige Cangrande, the riverbank on the castle side, and step back until the full span of arches and the castle fit in one frame. Guides often call this the signature view. An alternative is to walk onto the bridge itself. From there you get the crenellated brick walkway with the castle behind, and the Adige bending away towards Ponte Pietra. Take a few frames from each spot, because the two views are quite different. On the riverbank, keep an eye on passers-by so they don't wander into the edge of your shot.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Verona, where the Adige runs past the Castelvecchio fortress. The bridge links the castle side of the river with the opposite bank.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Castelvecchio area in the historic centre and walk to the Adige riverbank on the castle side, to Lungadige Cangrande. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the riverbank is narrow and you cannot step back far enough to fit the bridge and castle together. Where there is room, use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the arches and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lungadige Cangrande (riverbank on the castle side, downstream (east) of the bridge). The full arched span of the bridge in profile, with the Castelvecchio fortress rising behind it. The bridge lies to the south of you. Step back until the whole bridge and the castle sit in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the bridge's upper edge with a horizontal line so the walls don't look tilted. Put the arches in the lower half and let the castle towers fill the space above. For a second view, walk onto Ponte Scaligero itself and photograph the crenellated walkway with Castelvecchio behind, or the Adige curving towards Ponte Pietra.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the brick keeps its colour. Wipe your lens before shooting, as pocket lint softens the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the brick. After dark, night mode works if you rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep still.

text.access_note: The bridge is a free pedestrian crossing and the riverbank is a public street. The Castelvecchio Museum is ticketed, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Porta Borsari
label: Porta Borsari
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corso Cavour' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Corso Cavour nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138812787: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Porta Borsari' (14 m across).
notes: Roman city gate with a carved facade.

text.description: Porta Borsari is a Roman gate that once served as the main entrance to Verona. The front you see today is local white limestone. It has two arches with slim half-columns and decorated capitals, and above them a double band of twelve arched windows, some set in small niches with triangular tops. The gate dates to the 1st century AD, probably replacing an earlier gate from the century before, and an inscription records another rebuild in 265 AD. The Roman road known as the Via Postumia ran through it. The current name comes from the guard soldiers who were paid the dazio (bursarii). In the Middle Ages it was called Porta di San Zeno, and the Romans themselves called it Porta Iovia. It photographs well because the façade is flat, symmetrical and pale, so a straight-on shot looks tidy and every arch and window reads clearly. A street scene around it gives a good sense of scale. Step a little to either side for a slight angle if you want more depth. Come early in the morning if you can, as the area is busy at midday. Repair work has been reported on the gate, and scaffolding or covers can block parts of the view, so be ready to adapt your framing.
text.geographic_location: Porta Borsari is in Verona. It is the surviving face of the Roman city gate, and this façade faces Corso Cavour. Corso Porta Borsari offers a second vantage.
text.directions_text: Head for Corso Cavour in Verona and look for the gate's façade facing the street. No station or tram stop is listed close by, so follow the map on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too cramped to fit the upper windows in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the capitals and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Corso Cavour (facing the gate's façade from the Corso Cavour side). The single surviving face of the Roman gate, seen head-on from the street on the far side. From here you see the single surviving face of the Roman gate head-on, with both arches and the windows above.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre pillar between the arches up with the middle vertical line. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. Include a little of the street at the bottom for scale. For a second view, walk to Corso Porta Borsari for the full white façade with some street in the frame. Then go close with telephoto for the Corinthian capitals and the stone texture, letting the arch rise out of the top of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale limestone keeps its detail. Live Photos can help if people walk through the arches, as you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best, as the area is heavy with visitors at midday. Check current conditions first, because repair work can block some angles.

text.access_note: The gate is part of the street scene, but repair work has been reported, so check current conditions before you go.

name: Giardino Giusti
label: Giardino Giusti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Giardino Giusti' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Giardino Giusti' (way/564997764): middle (251 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/142873521: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo Giusti del Giardino' (97 m across).
notes: Renaissance garden with cypress avenue and a view of the city.

text.description:
Giardino Giusti is a Renaissance garden on a hillside in the east of Verona, laid out from 1580 and often called one of the finest Italian gardens. It sits behind the 16th-century Palazzo Giusti, a Mannerist building with a tower added in 1701. The garden is made of terraces climbing the hill, with a parterre, a hedge maze that was rebuilt after 1945, and a long cypress walk.

It photographs well because the climb pays off. At the top belvedere you look through a frame of dark cypresses to Verona's rooftops, bell towers and the Adige valley below. Several guides call this the most photogenic 'Verona from above' shot. On the way up, the straight cypress walk and the maze below make good extra shots.

One fact worth knowing: the Giusti family were allowed to add 'del Giardino' to their surname because the garden mattered so much. A severe storm in 2020 killed many trees, including the 600-year-old Goethe cypress, so don't look for it near the entrance. Take the main view from the top, then spend a few minutes on the alley and the maze. Rooftop views look best when the light is soft, so late afternoon is a good bet.
text.geographic_location: In the east of Verona, a short distance from Piazza Isolo and close to the city centre, on the hillside behind Palazzo Giusti.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop at this spot, so start from the Piazza Isolo area in the east of the city centre, a short distance from the garden. The Ponte Pietra riverside walk makes a pleasant approach on foot. Inside, the belvedere is about 2 minutes on foot from the palazzo in a straight line, so allow a little longer for the climb. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main rooftop view. Switch to 2x or 3x on a telephoto phone to pick out the bell towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the cypress alley and for the maze.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Giardino Giusti (upper belvedere at the top of the garden, reached by the climb past the cypresses). A cypress-framed foreground with Verona's rooftops, bell towers and the Adige valley spread out below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the cypresses as a dark frame at the edge of the picture and turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. For a different shot, look straight down the symmetrical cypress alley to the grotto and carved mask, or shoot from a high point down onto the maze pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and rooftops keep their colour. The cypress shade will then look dark, which suits the frame. Try panorama mode slowly for the wide valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light over the city is warmer. Check the official site for opening times.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed garden, so check the official site before you go for current opening times, ticket details and any photography rules (organised or professional shoots may need permission).

name: Verona Cathedral
label: Verona Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Duomo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Duomo' (way/24438670): middle (105 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1193534140: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cattedrale di Santa Maria Matricolare' (99 m across).
notes: Romanesque cathedral with a fine marble portal.

text.description: Verona Cathedral, also called the Duomo, is a Romanesque church dedicated to the Virgin Mary. It was built after an earthquake in 1117 destroyed two earlier churches on the site, and it was consecrated in 1187. It photographs well because the front is full of detail. The two-storey porch is carved with sculpture by the twelfth-century sculptor Nicholaus, and its portico rests on the backs of two griffins. Figures of Roland and Oliver stand in the walls either side of the doorway. Gothic windows and a later Baroque top section show how the building changed over the centuries. The bell tower was begun in the 16th century by Michele Sanmicheli and never finished. The best front view is from Piazza Duomo, where the small square and its surrounding buildings frame the facade and a bronze angel statue sits in view. Start with a wide shot of the whole front, then move in on the porch carvings. For a different view, the bell tower rises above the old town as seen from Ponte Pietra, and the free terrace at Castel San Pietro looks across the river and rooftops to the cathedral. Exterior photos are not affected by services, but check the official site before you go if you also want to see inside.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the old town of Verona, on and beside the small Piazza Duomo, with its main facade facing the square on the west side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby, so reach Piazza Duomo on foot from the centre of the old town. From there the cathedral is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the porch sculpture, the griffins and the angel statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Duomo (in front of the west facade). The Romanesque facade of the cathedral framed by the surrounding buildings of the small square, with the bronze angel statue in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central porch with the middle of the frame, keeping the phone level so the facade does not lean. Let the neighbouring buildings form a frame at the edges, and include the bronze angel statue if it is in view. For a second view, try the bell tower from Ponte Pietra, or the wider view from the Castel San Pietro terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale facade and sky keep their detail. For the carved details, zoom in with the telephoto instead of cropping later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing facade best, as the front catches warmer, lower light. Early morning is usually quieter for a shot without crowds.

text.access_note: The outside of the cathedral can be photographed from the open square, but it is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any dress code.

name: Castel San Pietro
label: Castel San Pietro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazzale Castel San Pietro' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazzale Castel San Pietro' (way/292288206): middle (68 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W142874973 (Castel San Pietro): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop viewpoint with the classic panorama of the old town.

text.description: Castel San Pietro stands on the hilltop above the Adige, and the open terrace in front of it gives one of the classic views of Verona. From the terrace you look over the historic centre. Ponte Pietra sits directly below, the river curves through the city, and the bell towers rise above the rooftops. On a clear day the Arena shows in the distance. The castle building is not open to visitors, so treat it as a backdrop. Guides describe the terrace as the standard postcard view of the city and a favourite spot for sunset, and it is free to enter. It can get crowded at busy times, so a little patience helps. Take the wide view first, then go in closer on the details: the bridge, the river bend, a single tower against the sky. If you want a calmer angle, several guides mention a brick wall or ramp near the restaurant at the top of the terrace. Look for it on the ground, as it isn't marked on the map. For a different view, photograph the castle hill from below at Ponte Pietra, or climb the Scalinata S. Pietro, where colourful houses and flowers frame the rising views of the city.
text.geographic_location: On the hill above the Adige, overlooking the historic centre of Verona, directly above Ponte Pietra. The terrace sits in front of the old barracks building at the top of the hill.
text.directions_text: Make for Ponte Pietra, at the foot of the hill, then climb the Scalinata S. Pietro staircase or take the funicular up to the terrace (check the official site for funicular times and tickets before you go). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full panorama, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the rooftops. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Ponte Pietra, the bell towers and the Arena in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Piazzale Castel San Pietro (open terrace in front of the barracks, on the hilltop). A wide panorama over the historic centre with Ponte Pietra directly below, the Adige curving through the city, the bell towers, and the Arena in the distance. The castle building is just to the north-west. For the castle itself, step a little way along the terrace and face it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the river bend along one of the lines so the curve leads the eye into the city. Include Ponte Pietra below as your anchor. Take one wide shot and one telephoto shot of the towers and the Arena. For a different angle, try the castle hill from Ponte Pietra below, or the colourful houses along the Scalinata S. Pietro.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest part of the city to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon and golden hour, staying on into blue hour. The terrace can get crowded at peak times, so arrive early for a good spot.

text.access_note: The terrace is open and free to enter, but don't expect to go inside the castle building, and check the official site before you go for funicular times and any restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Night mode shots are steadier if you brace your elbows against your body.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky colour at sunset.
The castle building is about 1 minute on foot from the stand-here point (43 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) can pick out the Arena and bell towers from the terrace.

name: Arco dei Gavi
label: Arco dei Gavi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arco dei Gavi' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/293954491: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Arco dei Gavi' (18 m across).

text.description:
The Arco dei Gavi is a Roman arch from the first half of the 1st century AD, built for the Gavia family, a noble line with roots in Verona. It is a rare example of a monumental arch paid for privately. Its story is unusual. In the Middle Ages it served as a city gate and was built into the Castelvecchio defences. French engineers took it apart in 1805, and it was rebuilt from the original stones and finished in 1932. It now stands in the small square beside Castelvecchio, close to the river Adige.

It photographs well because it is compact and clearly shaped, with pale stone, columns and niches that show up well on a phone screen. Most visitors shoot the front for the classic view. From the phone icon on the map you are at the rear side instead. From there the arch sits with the river, the small park beside it and the bridge behind, which makes a calmer picture with more sense of place.

The arch stands next to a busy street (Corso Cavour), so step back carefully and keep an eye on traffic while you frame the shot. If you also want the postcard view, walk round to the front and photograph the full arch and its columns. Another option is to look back at it across the Adige from Ponte Scaligero, with Castelvecchio in the background. Take care there, because the walkways are narrow and have no guardrails.
text.geographic_location: In the Castelvecchio area of Verona, in the small square next to Castelvecchio. The arch stands close to the Adige riverbank and beside Corso Cavour.
text.directions_text: Head for Castelvecchio, beside the Adige, as the arch stands in the small square right next to it. Once there, walk round to the river side of the arch, which is where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the arch, river and bridge sit together naturally. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the small park and riverbank are cramped. Use 2x telephoto for a tighter shot of the stonework and columns without moving closer to the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows a quieter view of the arch with the river, the small adjacent park and the bridge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch on one side, with the river and bridge filling the other. Keep the phone level so the columns stay upright. For the classic postcard view, walk round to the front and photograph the whole arch and its columns. Or try the view across the river from Ponte Scaligero, with Castelvecchio behind, but take care on its narrow walkways.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the bright sky or water. Take a few shots, because passing people and traffic change the scene quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when the stone looks warmer and the riverside feels calmer.

text.access_note: The arch is an open-air public monument that you can see from the street, but check the official site before you go in case anything has changed.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines and a lowered exposure slider help keep the pale stone detailed against a bright sky or water (general phone-photography advice).
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps in the cramped small park and riverbank area (general advice, not stated in the sources).
Passing people and traffic change the scene quickly, so taking several shots helps (general advice).

name: Scaliger Tombs
label: Scaliger Tombs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Arche Scaligere' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/347696754: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Arche Scaligere' (37 m across).
notes: Gothic funerary monuments of the Della Scala lords.

text.description:
The Scaliger Tombs are five Gothic funerary monuments for the Scaliger (Della Scala) family, who ruled Verona from the 13th to the late 14th century. They stand in a small court beside the church of Santa Maria Antica, behind a wall of wrought-iron grilles. The ironwork is decorated with a stair motif, a nod to the family name, which means 'of the stairs'. Most of the tombs are tall, open, tabernacle-like structures. Each has a sarcophagus under a carved canopy, topped by a statue of the dead lord on horseback in armour. Cangrande I's tomb was the first built, in the 14th century, and it sits over a doorway in the church wall. The equestrian statue you see on it is a copy, as the original is in the Castelvecchio museum.

This is a good phone subject because the carving is detailed and the stone is pale against the dark ironwork. The classic shot is taken through the grilles from the street. The enclosure itself is closed to visitors, so the railings give you a free, close look. Stand a little off-centre so that both the church wall and the pinnacles fit in the frame. Look up as well as ahead, because the best details, the canopies and the horsemen, are high above the street. Keep the grilles in the foreground as a dark frame, and be patient if other people are stopping to look.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Verona, in the small court beside the church of Santa Maria Antica. The tombs are reached from Via Arche Scaligere, close to the exit from Piazza dei Signori.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way to Piazza dei Signori in the historic centre of Verona. The phone icon on the map is on Via Arche Scaligere, at the corner by the piazza exit, by the grilles of the tombs. Once you are on the street, the iron grilles and the church wall are easy to see. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot of the grilles, the tombs and the church wall together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and carved canopies high up. Ultra-wide (0.5x) only helps if you want a very wide view of the street, and it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the Gothic tombs, their canopies and equestrian statues are framed through the dark ironwork against the pale stone and the church wall of Santa Maria Antica.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Move slightly off-centre so that both the church wall and the spires fit in the frame. Turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Take one wide shot with the grilles as a frame, then a zoomed shot of a single horseman.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the tomb to focus, not the bars, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the dark ironwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives warmer light and deeper shadows, according to one photography guide. Another suggests late morning for more balanced light.

text.access_note: The tomb enclosure is not open to visitors, so you look in through the iron grilles from the street. Access may change, so check current information locally before you visit.
claims_not_in_sources: The ironwork can confuse a phone's autofocus, so tapping on the stone to focus helps.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can stretch the edges of the frame in a narrow street.
Other visitors may stop at the grilles to look and take photos.

name: Roman Theatre of Verona
label: Roman Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte Pietra' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte Pietra' (way/1525501040): middle (74 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23164352: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Teatro Romano' (170 m across).
notes: 1st-century BC theatre on the hillside above the river.

text.description:
The Roman Theatre of Verona is an ancient theatre built into the hillside on the far bank of the Adige, just across the river from the old centre. It dates from the late 1st century BC. Today you can see the remains uncovered from around 1830: the curved seating (the cavea), steps, several arcades of the loggias and parts of the stage. A church, S. Siro, was built over part of the seating in the 10th century and restored in the 14th.

It photographs well because the terraced hillside rises straight up from the water. From Ponte Pietra you can fit the theatre, the Santo Stefano church and the curve of the river into one frame, which guides treat as the classic view. It is a free place to stand, and a short walk from the old centre. Walls were built along the Adige here in Roman times to guard against floods, so the river and theatre have long belonged together.

For a different angle, the terrace at Piazzale Castel San Pietro looks down on the theatre, with Ponte Pietra, the river bend and the old-town rooftops beyond. From the upper rows inside the theatre you can frame the stone seating with the city behind. Be aware that scaffolding and summer seating were reported over the cavea recently, so the steps may be partly hidden when you visit.
text.geographic_location: On the far bank of the Adige from the old centre of Verona, on the hillside just above the river and beside Ponte Pietra.
text.directions_text: Start from the old centre of Verona. Walk from the old centre to the old-town end of Ponte Pietra. From there the theatre is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the theatre, the church and the river together. Switch to 2x or more to pick out the rows of the cavea, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are on the riverbank steps and want the whole hillside from a low angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte Pietra (stand mid-bridge or on the bridge's old-town end and face east toward the theatre; the riverbank steps on the city side give a lower angle). The theatre's hillside cavea rising behind the river, with the Santo Stefano church and the curve of the Adige in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the river along the lower third, with the hillside filling the middle and upper part. Keep the horizon level so the bridge arches do not look tilted. If you want a high view instead, Piazzale Castel San Pietro shows the theatre below with Ponte Pietra and the old town beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hillside to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few frames, as people often walk across the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Several guides suggest sunset for the light on the river. One guide prefers the Castel San Pietro terrace at sunrise.

text.access_note: Ponte Pietra and the riverbank are open public spaces, but the theatre's upper terraces and museum are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica of San Zeno
label: San Zeno
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Zeno' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Zeno' (way/166325150): middle (119 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/288170289: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of San Zeno' (102 m across).
notes: Romanesque basilica with a rose window and bronze doors.

text.description:
The Basilica of San Zeno is a Romanesque church in the San Zeno district of Verona, and it is considered one of the masterpieces of medieval architecture. It stands on a site where at least five earlier religious buildings had stood, going back to a church over the tomb of Saint Zeno, who died between 372 and 380. The Romanesque rebuilding began around the end of the 11th century. The 1117 earthquake interrupted the work, but by about 1138 much of the present church was finished.

For a phone photo, the draw is the rose-coloured facade with the bell tower beside it, seen across Piazza San Zeno with its cafés and old buildings at the edges. The large rose window, known as the "Wheel of Fortune" and carved by Brioloto de Balneo, is the detail that catches the eye. The bronze panels of the portal are also famous, so there is plenty to zoom in on. The square gives the standard straight-on view, and the facade fills the frame without much effort.

For a different angle, the church steps give a closer, slightly higher view of the entrance. Rigaste San Zeno, beside the Adige, is a quieter walk with historic buildings. Treat it as a scenic stroll rather than a sure shot of the church. Photography inside is generally allowed without flash, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of the San Zeno district of Verona, facing Piazza San Zeno, with the bell tower beside the church.
text.directions_text: Head for the San Zeno district of Verona; no station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so plan to walk in or use your own navigation to Piazza San Zeno. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the facade and bell tower. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you step in close and want the whole front in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and the portal.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Zeno (in front of the west facade). The rose-coloured facade and the bell tower, framed by the square's cafés and historic buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the facade up with the central vertical, keeping your phone level so the front does not lean. Include a little of the square's buildings at the edge to give a sense of place. For a second view, climb the church steps for a close, slightly raised shot of the entrance with the ultra-wide, or walk to Rigaste San Zeno for a quieter scene by the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale facade to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the rose-coloured stone keeps its detail against a bright sky. Hold still when you zoom in on the rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing facade best. Earlier in the day the square tends to be calmer, which makes a clear view easier.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica is a place of worship that may charge for entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sant'Anastasia
label: Sant'Anastasia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Sant'Anastasia' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Sant'Anastasia' (way/24893213): middle (58 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1193522172: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di Sant'Anastasia' (117 m across).
notes: Large Gothic church, the biggest in the city.

text.description:
Sant'Anastasia is the biggest and grandest church in Verona, and its red-brick Gothic front is a good subject for a phone. The facade was never finished, so the brickwork is left bare. The one flourish is a majestic Gothic doorway. Beside it you can pick out the little Church of San Giorgetto and the Castelbarco tomb, which add character to a wider shot.

The Dominican friars were given the land in 1260. Building began in 1290 and dragged on for generations, and the church was consecrated on 22 October 1471. It stands at the end of the decumanus maximus, the main street of Roman Verona, close to the bend of the Adige river by Ponte Pietra. Inside, it is known for its chapels and paintings by well-known Veronese artists, but this spot is about the outside.

The usual postcard angle is from the western side of Piazza Sant'Anastasia, looking straight at the facade. The warm brick looks good against the sky, and the square gives you enough room to fit the whole front in. For a different view, try Ponte Nuovo, where you can see the basilica and its bell tower across the river. Expect other visitors in the square, so be patient and wait for a gap in the crowd. The church is closed at some times for services, so look at the facade first and go in only if it is open.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Verona, on Piazza Sant'Anastasia, a short walk from the Adige river and Ponte Pietra.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. If you are near Ponte Pietra or the river bend, the church is close by. Otherwise, go by taxi or hired scooter to Piazza Sant'Anastasia in the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole facade and some of the square in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Gothic doorway and the brick detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Sant'Anastasia (western side of the square, facing the church facade). The red-brick Gothic facade of the basilica, with the Church of San Giorgetto and the Castelbarco tomb visible alongside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the facade up with them. Hold the phone level and upright, since tilting it back makes the building lean. Keep the doorway near the centre, and include a little of the square in the foreground for scale. For a second view, try Ponte Nuovo, looking across the Adige to the basilica and its bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the brick keeps its colour. Panorama is better avoided here, as it can bend the straight lines of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day, when the square is usually quieter. Use soft, even light on the brick and avoid harsh midday glare if you can.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the open public square, but the church is a place of worship that is closed at some times for services, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Fermo Maggiore
label: San Fermo Maggiore
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Castel San Pietro' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Castel San Pietro' (way/142874973): middle (106 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/358970376: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di San Fermo Maggiore' (82 m across).
notes: Two-level church, Romanesque below and Gothic above.

text.description: San Fermo Maggiore is a Romanesque and Gothic church in central Verona, dedicated to Saints Firmus and Rusticus, two brothers remembered as local martyrs from the 3rd century. A church is thought to have stood here since the 8th century. By the 11th century the Benedictines had added an upper storey and a bell tower, and the campanile was only finished in the 13th century. The roofline with its pinnacles is the part that most rewards a photograph. The interior holds medieval frescos and the Brenzoni Monument, with a fresco of the Annunciation by Pisanello above it. From there you get a broad view over the old town, with Ponte Pietra, the cathedral and the river. The church lies about 1 km to the south, so it may be a small part of a wide scene, or hard to see at all. Take the wide view first, then, if you can pick out the church, zoom in on it. If you want the church as the main subject, Ponte Navi gives a river-side view of it with its tall bell tower. The terrace is reached on foot by steps, so wear comfortable shoes.
text.geographic_location: San Fermo Maggiore stands in central Verona, near the Adige.
text.directions_text: The church itself is about 1 km to the south of the terrace. To photograph it from Ponte Navi instead, walk down towards the river and follow the Adige. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole panorama. Then, if you can pick out the church, switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to zoom in on it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a sweeping view of the whole bend of the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Castel San Pietro (the hillside terrace above the Adige, reached on foot from the north end of Ponte Pietra). A broad panorama of the old town, with Ponte Pietra, the cathedral and the river; the church of San Fermo sits at the foot of this hill, though no page confirms it is clearly visible in the frame. If it is hard to see, Ponte Navi gives a clearer view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the river on a lower line, with the rooftops filling the middle and sky above. If the church is visible, zoom in on it for a second shot. For a closer, church-focused view from the river, Ponte Navi is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooftops to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone against a wall or rail when you zoom, to keep it steady.

text.access_note: The terrace is reached on foot by steps, but the church is a place of worship and may have visiting rules and fees, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The church may appear small in a wide view from the terrace, and visibility of San Fermo from the terrace is not confirmed.
Looking south from the terrace, the church lies in the direction of the old town rooftops.
Sunrise and golden hour light usually suits a panorama like this.
Phones tend to blur when zoomed unless they are steadied, so resting against a wall or rail helps.
